lesson.intro: Hari terakhir bukan akhir dari belajar. Ini saatnya menyusun rencana yang bisa kamu jalankan sendiri, dengan prioritas yang jelas dan tinjauan rutin.

sections.heading: Menulis komitmen
sections.bodyMd: Buat **commitment** yang spesifik, misalnya belajar 20 menit setiap pagi. Tulis dengan kalimat sederhana dan letakkan di tempat yang sering kamu lihat.

sections.heading: Menentukan prioritas
sections.bodyMd: Pilih satu atau dua **priority** untuk bulan berikutnya. Dengan begitu energi belajarmu tidak terpecah ke terlalu banyak tujuan.

sections.heading: Menjaga kebiasaan
sections.bodyMd: **Discipline** berarti kembali ke kebiasaan dengan cepat setelah hari yang terlewat. Gunakan **reminder** untuk membantu kamu mengingatnya.

sections.heading: Meninjau dan merayakan
sections.bodyMd: Setiap minggu, gunakan **checkpoint** untuk melihat kemajuan. Jika kamu merasa **accountable** kepada orang lain, tinjauan akan lebih mudah dijalankan. Jangan lupa **celebrate** pencapaian kecil.

block3.title: Merencanakan Langkah Setelah Program
block3.text:
Ending a learning programme is a good moment to look back and plan forward. The final day is not the end of progress. It is a checkpoint, a place to review what you have achieved and to decide how you will sustain your habits. Many learners stop when the programme ends, so a clear plan matters.

Commitment is the first ingredient. A commitment is a promise you make to yourself about a specific action, such as studying for twenty minutes every morning. Write it down in simple words, and place it where you will see it each day. A vague goal like 'speak better' is hard to measure, while a clear commitment can be checked.

Discipline is what keeps the commitment alive on difficult days. Discipline does not mean never missing a session. It means returning to the habit quickly after a missed day. Learners who show discipline often plan small routines, such as reviewing vocabulary during a coffee break.

Setting priority is equally important. Not every skill needs the same attention. A learner who wants to pass an exam may place speaking first, while a learner who reads English for work may focus on reading. Choose two or three priorities and keep the rest for later, so that your energy is not spread too thin.

To sustain progress, build a simple weekly review. Every seven days, check your notes, count completed sessions, and identify one area that needs more time. A reminder on your phone can help, but the most useful reminder is a short note that asks what you learned this week. This keeps the habit visible and honest.

Being accountable also helps. You can share your plan with a friend, a teacher, or a study group, and ask them to check your progress. When someone else knows your goal, it becomes easier to follow through. Accountability is not about judgement. It is about support and honest feedback.

Small wins deserve attention too. When you finish a difficult week, take time to celebrate. Celebrating does not need to be expensive. It can be a short walk, a favourite meal, or simply a moment of pride in your work. Positive feelings make the next cycle of learning more enjoyable.

Finally, write a pledge for the next stage. A pledge is a short statement that combines your priorities, your routine, and your review date. For example, 'For the next month, I will practise speaking three times a week, and I will review my progress every Sunday.' This statement gives you a clear direction.

The most important goal is continuity. A learner who keeps a modest routine for a long time usually makes more progress than someone who studies intensely for a few days and then stops. Continuity turns learning into a lasting habit, and that habit is the real result of this programme.
